column121: I was PIC for the flight tests during the incident; with the aircraft used during this flight; which is a homebuilt prototype by the owning company (I work for). The aircraft was modified with radio control ability (a radio control receiver (RX)) for manual injection of a PIC actioned failure using a handheld radio control transmitter (TX); as well as for an additional operational risk mitigation to switch to manual attitude control mode; from automated control mode. This incident did not cause any property damage or injuries.During an automated mission takeoff there was an unintentional actuation of the incorrect transmitter switch. The intention was to use the failure injection switch command; though the unintentional action toggled the manual attitude mode takeover switch instead. The unintentional action caused personal confusion; causing the aircraft to make a ground impact; under power; and then climb at maximum throttle setting; without any control authority from the radio TX controller. After exhausting all control options at my disposal (manual and automated system) and knowing once switched to attitude mode there is no returning to automated mode; I stated I had lost control to the flight crew. The aircraft climbed to a point where it then shifted to descend and had an attitude controlled landing in a field. Upon aircraft retrieval onsite inspection; it was found that the radio control RX unit was disconnected from the leads to the flight controller; and damaged where the lead plugs into the unit. The initial ground contact is thought to be the cause of the RX unit system disconnect. Aircraft logs found that the maximum altitude reached was 1265.4 ft AGL. The aircraft maintained last commanded throttle input from the radio control; after the link was lost.The previous days/weeks leading up to this date caused higher stress levels to myself; and teammates. I believe this is a factor which helped lead to my temporary confusion causing the unintentional action.Mitigations have been reviewed and actioned into place:1)  The aircraft flight controller system has an addition of an attitude flight mode Link Lost timer to actuate after a specific amount of time. This is in addition to an automated flight mode timer; already in place. The flight controller also now has adjusted throttle settings when a link is lost.2) The procedure to adhere the manual radio control receiver has been reviewed and improved; adding multiple layers of adhesion.I am confident this instance of a fly away risk has been mitigated.

column121: An autonomous 2D mapping mission was being conducted over a campus; to include the park immediately to the south of the campus; by the drone unit of the Local Police Department.  The mapping route was set up in the control software; FreeFlight 7 for single pass 2D mapping. The drone passed preflight checks and was operating normally upon launch. The drone launched upon command; rose to 150' AGL; then flew to the furthest point away to begin gathering data.  The drone flew 4 passes of the planned 14 and was lost.  Visual contact was lost and the link with the controller; which had been showing the camera view and GPS location of the drone; was lost at the same time.No anomalies were observed in the drone's flight path or camera operation.  The controller had a solid link to the drone; and no warnings displayed at any time.  The controller and drone batteries were both over 90% of full at the time of the incident.The drone has not been located or recovered to date.It is believed the drone experienced a catastrophic failure of a critical system such as the battery; control circuitry; or a motor causing the loss.No damage or injuries are believed to have been caused by this incident.

column121: Person A conducted a Small Unmanned Aircraft System (sUAS) Pilot Flight Evaluation using corporate-owned asset; a Skydio S2. Person B and Person C  served as sUAS Technicians (trainees); while Person D acted as the sUAS Check Pilot. Person E served as the sUAS Technician; and Person F served as the Flight Release Officer. The evaluation took place at Location X The UAS Organizational Risk Management Matrix score was 19 (low risk). Flight release was approved. A pre-flight inspection was completed using the sUAS Checklist. Battery 17-BATT-4 was installed and measured 99 percent charge at takeoff at XA23L. Person A began the flight by performing half-stick maneuvers and system checks; all of which were normal. The aircraft then ascended to 25 feet AGL and executed straight-and-level; square-pattern; and point-of-interest maneuvers. Approximately four minutes into the flight; Person A handed the controller to Person  D so she could reposition the aircraft to an area suitable for the recovery-from-unusual-attitude maneuver. About 90 seconds later; the iPad display went black while the battery remained at 78 percent. Person D announced 'Lost link' three times at XA28L; five minutes into the sortie. The sUAS automatically ascended to between 100 and 150 feet AGL. At that moment; the Pilot in Command's position was Location Y; and the sUAS position was Location Z; a distance of approximately 120 feet. The PIC attempted to manually return the aircraft to the home point but was unable to control ascent or descent functions. The aircraft autonomously initiated return-to-home and descended over the landing area while the iPad screen remained blank. After cycling the iPad's power; the display returned; but connection to the sUAS could not be re-established. The sUAS hovered over the home point at roughly 5 feet AGL; then gradually descended to 2 feet AGL and self-landed after approximately 90 seconds. Video recording stopped at 6 minutes 12 seconds; and total flight time was 7 minutes (0.08 hours). The battery charge prior to the lost link event was 78 percent. Post-flight observations noted that the iPad had 83 percent battery at XD16L; while sUAS Battery 17-BATT-4 measured 56 percent at XD19L. The iPad displayed a 'storage full' warning; indicating low available memory. No equipment damage or personnel injury occurred during this sortie.

column121: On Day 4; at approximately XA:00 local time; a recreational small UAS flight occurred with my DJI Mavic 4 Pro near Location X. I registered the UAS and completed my TRUST Completion Certificate on Day 0. This occurred during my first week as a new recreational UAS flyer while I was still learning the FAA rules; airspace requirements; and aircraft/controller settings.During the flight; two family members manipulated the controls at different times. I was not physically manipulating the controls at the time of the altitude deviation. However; I was the registered owner and was supervising the flight; and I did not prevent or correct the altitude increase quickly enough.The DJI flight record showed a maximum altitude of approximately 3;250 feet AGL relative to the takeoff/home point. This is my best estimate based on the available flight record. The flight was recreational; and the altitude deviation was not intentional. At the time; I believed the flight was being conducted from a private/open area; but I now understand that private property does not determine airspace authorization and that I must verify airspace; airport proximity; and altitude limits before every flight.I am not aware of any aircraft conflict; near-miss; collision; injury; flyaway; lost link; or evasive action.I believe the contributing factors were human factors; inexperience; insufficient monitoring of altitude; allowing untrained people to manipulate the controls; and misunderstanding of the aircraft/controller settings and altitude limitations.After this event; I reviewed the recreational UAS rules more carefully and took corrective action. I contacted DJI for assistance with the controller and aircraft safety settings. I learned how to set maximum altitude and distance limits and how to lock the controller so another person cannot use it without a code.To prevent recurrence; I will not allow any untrained person to manipulate the controls. Before every flight; I will verify airspace; airport proximity; altitude limits; weather; and the flight location; obtain any required FAA authorization; maintain visual line of sight; monitor altitude continuously; use altitude and distance limits in the controller; keep the controller locked from unauthorized use; and stop the flight if I am not fully sure it can be conducted safely and legally.I completed this report to the best of my knowledge using my recollection and the DJI flight record/controller information available to me. Some details; including the exact time and maximum altitude; are approximate based on the available record. My goal in filing this report is to be transparent about the safety issue and to help prevent it from happening again.

I launched my DJI Mavic 3 Pro for a recreational flight under the recreational exception to capture video of Location Y over the river.The flight was conducted during daylight in clear weather. The aircraft did not return home; and I was unable to re-establish communication or control. The aircraft was subsequently lost in the river. No injuries or third-party property damage occurred.After the incident; responding law enforcement officers informed me that the area was subject to a Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR). At the time of the flight; I was not aware that a TFR was in effect. I fully cooperated with the responding officers throughout the encounter.I hold both an FAA TRUST certificate and an FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate. Because this flight was conducted solely for recreational purposes; I was operating under the recreational exception.This event reinforced the importance of verifying Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs) and current airspace status immediately before every flight. As an out-of-state recreational pilot visiting Location X; I learned that I should verify current FAA airspace information; including Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs); before every flight regardless of location.

column121: I was operating a DJI M30T and had just taken off at a beach location when at around 25' AGL the drone decided to take off vertically and I lost all control of the drone. The sticks were unresponsive. I force closed DroneSense; which was the app we fly in and entered the DJI Pilot app. While in this app; I was still unable to control the drone. I attempted to place the drone into RTH without success; the RTH initiated but did not respond. I also attempted to place the drone in Attitude Mode (ATTI); which also did not work. I then proceeded to toggle on and off the bottom Vision Positioning System (VPS) sensor; which was already off. After this; I attempted to regain control again and attempted to initiate another Return to Home. This time the drone responded; and I took over and landed the drone without further incident. The drone reached a max Alt of 1276 ft/389 meters AGL. The drone was only about 50 ft Horizontally away from me. We were in the process of calling ZZZ Tower when control was regained and the drone was landed. Camera feed was never lost during the incident. DroneSense replay shows stick inputs in an attempt to take control without any luck.
